evidence: Cic. Par. 45: paupertātem vel potius egestātem ac mendīcitātem (Lewis & Short)
Ov. Met. 8.633: paupertātemque fatendō effēcēre levem
terms.comment: Slender means rather than want, the opposite of riches (Lewis & Short); real need is egestās.

evidence: Verg. G. 1.146: dūrīs urgēns in rēbus egestās, want that presses in hard times
Publ. I 7: Inopiae dēsunt multa, avāritiae omnia, poverty lacks much, greed everything

terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Hor., Verg.; in prose after Augustus

phrases.latin: sed pia Baucis anus parilīque aetāte Philēmōn illā sunt annīs jūnctī juvenālibus, illā cōnsenuēre casā paupertātemque fatendō effēcēre levem nec inīquā mente ferendō
phrases.english: but good old Baucis and Philemon, of the same age, were married in that cottage in their young years and grew old in it; they made their poverty light by owning it and bearing it without complaint

phrases.latin: vetus est prōverbium: paupertātem certissimam esse, cum alicujus indigeat, ūtī eō nōn posse, quia ignōrētur, ubi prōjectum jaceat, quod dēsīderātur
phrases.english: there is an old proverb that the surest poverty is to need something and be unable to use it, because no one knows where the thing you want has been thrown
